groups.high: Non-refoulement prohibits return to specified threats to life or freedom under Article 33 of the 1951 Refugee Convention. The protected grounds are race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group, and political opinion. Protection cannot depend solely on whether a government has already formally recognized refugee status; otherwise removal before assessment could defeat the safeguard. It covers direct removal and transfer where onward return creates the prohibited risk. Conflict does not automatically establish refugee status, but persecution during conflict can qualify; personal targeting by name is not indispensable where group membership establishes the risk. Article 33(2) contains narrow exceptions for reasonable grounds of danger to the host state's security, or a final conviction for a particularly serious crime combined with danger to the community. That is distinct from Article 1F exclusion for certain pre-admission crimes. Do not describe the Convention exception as simply any serious nonpolitical crime. Separate human-rights obligations prohibit removal to torture and may continue to bar return even where a Convention exception is established. Calling every form of refugee non-refoulement an uncontested absolute jus cogens rule obscures these distinctions. Border screening, interception, detention, and third-country transfer policies must not circumvent the applicable protection. Assess the individual's circumstances and available protection before removal, with access to an effective procedure. The Convention principally concerns people outside their own country; internally displaced people have other protections.
groups.mid: Non-refoulement is the ban on sending a refugee back to a threat to life or freedom. Article 33 of the 1951 Refugee Convention gives five grounds: race, religion, nationality, a particular social group, and political opinion. A person may be a refugee before a state confirms it. Officials must assess the risk before removal. Sending someone to a third country may also break the rule if that country sends them on to danger. War alone does not decide a claim. But persecution in war can qualify, and being part of a targeted group may be enough; a person need not be named on a threat list. Article 33(2) has narrow exceptions. One concerns danger to the host state's security. The other requires a final conviction for a particularly serious crime together with a continuing danger to the community, rather than simply a general allegation of wrongdoing. This is not the same as Article 1F exclusion. An ordinary offense does not automatically establish either exception or remove the state's remaining human-rights obligations. Separate human-rights rules ban return to torture, even when a Convention exception applies. Calling the whole rule absolute hides these legal differences. Border checks, detention, sea interceptions, and transfers abroad must not avoid protection duties. Each person needs a fair assessment and an effective way to seek protection. People who flee inside their own country usually have other protections, rather than Convention refugee status.
groups.low: Non-refoulement means not sending a refugee back to danger. Article 33 of the 1951 Refugee Convention guards life and freedom. The threat must relate to race, religion, nationality, a particular social group, or political opinion. Officials may not yet have confirmed refugee status. They still need to assess the risk before return. They must also check if a third country might send the person on to danger. War alone does not settle a claim. But persecution in war can count. Being part of a targeted group may put a person at risk even if no threat names them. Article 33(2) has narrow exceptions. One is danger to the host state's security. The other needs a final conviction for a particularly serious crime and danger to the community. Article 1F has different exclusion rules. An ordinary crime does not by itself allow return. Separate human-rights rules still ban return to torture. That can be true even when a Convention exception applies. So calling every part of the rule absolute can mislead. Border checks, detention, boats stopped at sea, and transfers abroad must respect these duties. People need a fair assessment and a way to seek protection that works. People who flee within their own country have other protections.
groups.source_review: Article33 text and distinction from1F checked against Convention; torture nonreturn treated separately, not as unrestricted33(2) permission.
groups.notes: Corrected exception and absolute/jus-cogens assertions; removed named-individual-targeting requirement.

groups.high: Article 1A(2) of the 1951 Refugee Convention, read with the 1967 Protocol, defines a refugee through a well-founded fear of persecution connected to race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group, or political opinion. The person must be outside their country of nationality and unable or, because of that fear, unwilling to obtain its protection. For a stateless person, the corresponding reference is the country of former habitual residence and inability or fear-based unwillingness to return. An asylum seeker requests international protection and awaits a decision; this is not synonymous with a voluntary economic migrant. Recognition is declaratory: a person who meets the definition is a refugee before formal recognition. The Protocol removed the original pre-1951 temporal limitation and generally removed geographic limitations, while allowing certain pre-existing geographic declarations to continue. Armed conflict, generalized violence, and disasters are not automatic substitutes for the Convention's criteria, although conflict-related persecution can meet them and regional or complementary protection may be broader. Non-refoulement guards against return to relevant threats, subject to the distinct rules of refugee and human-rights law. Convention rights include education, employment, documentation, public assistance, and movement, but their precise scope depends on the relevant article and attachment to the state, not a single unconditional package. Refugees must respect host-country laws under Article 2. Exclusion and cessation provisions also require assessment. The definition is a legal protection framework, not a guarantee of citizenship or automatic approval of every asylum application.
groups.mid: A refugee has crossed a border and has a well-founded fear of persecution. Article 1A(2) of the 1951 Refugee Convention links that fear to race, religion, nationality, a particular social group, or political opinion. The person cannot, or because of the fear will not, seek their own country's protection. For a stateless person, the rule refers to the country where they formerly lived and whether they can safely return. An asylum seeker is someone asking for protection while a decision is pending. They are not simply an economic migrant. Formal recognition confirms refugee status; it does not create the fear or make someone a refugee for the first time. The 1967 Protocol removed the old pre-1951 time limit. It generally removed the place limit too. Some older geographic declarations could remain. War, widespread violence, or a disaster does not automatically meet every Convention test. Persecution in a war can still qualify. Regional rules and other forms of protection may cover more people. Non-refoulement limits return to danger, with separate refugee and human-rights rules. Refugees have rights to matters such as school, work, documents, public aid, and movement. Each article sets its own conditions for rights. The person's situation in the country matters too. Article 2 also requires respect for the host country's laws. Exclusion rules and rules ending status must be considered where relevant. Refugee status does not itself give citizenship or guarantee that every asylum claim will succeed.
groups.low: A refugee is outside their own country. They fear serious mistreatment. The fear must be well founded. Article 1A(2) of the 1951 Refugee Convention gives five grounds: race, religion, nationality, a particular social group, or political opinion. The person cannot get their country's protection, or fears doing so. If a person has no nationality, the rule looks at where they used to live and whether they can return. An asylum seeker asks for safety and awaits a decision. They are not simply moving for a better job. A person who meets the refugee test is a refugee before officials confirm it. The decision recognizes the status. The 1967 Protocol removed the old pre-1951 time limit. It generally removed the place limit too, though some older declarations could stay. War, violence, or disaster does not settle each claim on its own. Persecution in war can count. Regional rules or other forms of protection may cover more people. Non-refoulement guards against return to danger. Refugee law and human-rights law have separate rules for it. Rights can include school, work, papers, public aid, and movement. Each article sets its own scope. Each right has its own terms. Article 2 says refugees must obey the host country's laws. Some people may be excluded. Status may end under set rules. It is not automatic citizenship, and not every claim will succeed.
groups.source_review: Definition, Protocol scope and declaration caveat checked; benefits described subject to their treaty conditions.
groups.notes: Corrected asylum-seeker/economic-migrant conflation, constitutive-recognition claim, and absolute removal of all geographical reservations.

groups.high: UDHR Article 14 recognizes the right to seek and enjoy asylum in other countries from persecution. The 1948 Declaration is not itself a treaty granting an unconditional entitlement to admission or asylum in a chosen country. Binding obligations arise through applicable treaties, customary rules, regional instruments, and domestic law. Protection is not limited to political activists: refugee persecution may relate to race, religion, nationality, a particular social group, or political opinion under the 1951 Convention. Article 14(2) prevents reliance on the asylum right in prosecutions genuinely arising from nonpolitical crimes or acts contrary to UN purposes and principles. The word genuinely matters: a fabricated criminal charge used to punish protected activity should not simply be accepted at face value. Convention exclusion provisions, including Article 1F, are separate and require their own legal assessment; not every accusation or minor offense automatically excludes someone. Non-refoulement restricts return to danger, and the absolute human-rights prohibition on return to torture must be assessed even when refugee status is excluded. Exclusion is therefore not automatic permission to deport or extradite. An asylum seeker should have access to a fair procedure in which risks, evidence, and legal grounds can be examined. Article 13's right to leave a country is related but does not itself compel another state to grant entry. The practical aim is effective protection rather than treating asylum as impunity for crime or as a benefit limited to one political category.
groups.mid: Article 14 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights protects seeking and enjoying asylum abroad from persecution. The Declaration was adopted in 1948. It is not a treaty that promises entry into any country of your choice. Other treaties, international rules, regional law, and national law set duties in more detail. Asylum is not just for political activists. The 1951 Refugee Convention lists race, religion, nationality, a particular social group, and political opinion as grounds. Article 14(2) has limits for prosecutions genuinely based on nonpolitical crimes or acts against UN purposes and principles. A false charge used to punish someone's beliefs must not be accepted without checking. Article 1F of the Convention has separate exclusion rules. A mere charge or minor offense does not automatically bar a person. Officials must also assess return to danger. Human-rights law bans sending someone to torture, even if they are excluded from refugee status. Exclusion is not automatic permission for deportation or extradition. A fair process lets the person explain the risk and show evidence. Article 13 protects leaving a country too, but does not force every other state to admit the person. Asylum aims to offer safety from persecution. It is not a free pass for crime or a right limited to one kind of political opponent.
groups.low: Article 14 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights says you can seek asylum in another country. That means asking for safety from persecution. The Declaration dates from 1948. It is not a treaty that promises entry to any country you choose. Other laws set each state's duties. Asylum is not just for people who oppose a government. The 1951 Refugee Convention lists race, religion, nationality, a particular social group, and political opinion. Article 14(2) sets limits. It concerns cases truly based on nonpolitical crimes or acts against UN purposes and principles. A false charge used to punish someone's views needs a proper check. Article 1F has separate rules for excluding people. A charge or minor offense does not by itself end a claim. Even if a person is excluded, officials must assess the risk of return. Human-rights law bans return to torture. Exclusion does not mean the person can just be sent away. Extradition still needs a proper legal check. A fair process lets them explain the danger and show proof. Officials need to check the facts, not just rely on a charge's label. Article 13 protects leaving a country, but does not make every other state let you in. Asylum is safety from persecution, not a way to escape all punishment for crime.
groups.source_review: UDHR14 and distinct Refugee Convention exclusion framework checked; no claim of automatic asylum/admission or automatic removal after exclusion.
groups.notes: Corrected blanket thief/fraud exclusion and return permission; protected grounds not limited to political persecution.

groups.high: Article 17, not Article 18, of the 1951 Refugee Convention governs wage-earning employment. It requires Contracting States to give refugees lawfully staying in their territory the most favorable treatment accorded to nationals of a foreign country in the same circumstances regarding access to paid employment. The attachment requirement and comparable circumstances matter: this is not an unconditional promise that every asylum seeker can take every job without a permit. Article 17(2) removes certain labor-market protective restrictions for refugees already exempt when the Convention took effect for that state, or who meet one of three conditions: three years' residence; a spouse with the country's nationality, provided the refugee has not abandoned that spouse; or one or more children with that nationality. Article 17(3) asks states to consider sympathetically bringing refugee employment rights into line with those of nationals. Article 18 separately concerns self-employment; Article 19 concerns liberal professions. These distinctions prevent confusing paid work with an unrestricted right to any profession or public office. Work permits, qualifications, and sectoral rules need assessment under the applicable provisions and domestic implementation, including any relevant treaty reservations. Compare the refugee's treatment with the correct foreign-national benchmark rather than assuming citizen parity. Meaningful access to lawful work supports self-reliance and reduces exploitation, but the Convention's exact conditions should not be replaced by broad statements of automatic universal labor-market access.
groups.mid: Article 17 of the 1951 Refugee Convention covers paid work. It applies to refugees lawfully staying in a state. They must get the best treatment given to nationals of a foreign country in the same circumstances. The right groups and conditions must be compared. It does not mean every asylum seeker can take any job without a permit. Some limits on foreign workers aim to protect the local job market. Those limits must not apply if the refugee was already exempt when the treaty took effect there. They also must not apply after three years of residence. Other routes are a spouse with the host country's nationality, if the refugee has not abandoned that spouse, or a child with that nationality. Article 17 asks states to consider rights closer to those of citizens too. Article 18 deals with working for yourself. Article 19 covers qualified professions. These are separate rules. A right to paid work does not open every public post or profession. Check local permit rules, required skills, sector limits, and any treaty reservation that matters. Compare the correct groups under the same conditions, rather than assuming full equality with citizens. Access to lawful work helps people support themselves and avoid abuse.
groups.low: Article 17 of the 1951 Refugee Convention covers paid jobs. It is for refugees lawfully staying in a country. They must get the best treatment given to people from a foreign state. The circumstances must be the same. This is not a promise of any job with no permit for every asylum seeker. Some limits protect the local job market. They must not apply to a refugee already exempt when the treaty took effect there. They must not apply after three years living in the country either. A spouse with the country's nationality is another route. The refugee must not have abandoned that spouse. Having a child with that nationality is another route. Article 17 asks states to consider job rights closer to those of citizens. Article 18 covers working for yourself. Article 19 covers qualified professions. The rules differ. Paid work rights do not open every public job or profession. Check permits and skills rules. Check limits for each kind of job too. A treaty reservation may also matter. Make a fair comparison with the right group. Use the same conditions. Do not assume the rules are always the same as citizens' rights. Lawful work helps people meet their needs and avoid abuse.
groups.source_review: Article17 including lawful-stay qualification and17(2) exceptions checked directly; Article18/19 distinguished.
groups.notes: Corrected Article18 misattribution and unconditional all-asylum-seeker/all-job parity claims.

groups.high: Article 27 of the 1951 Refugee Convention requires Contracting States to issue identity papers to refugees in their territory who lack a valid travel document. Unlike several other provisions, its text does not make lawful stay a prerequisite. The obligation should not be rewritten as applying only after a formal recognition ceremony or as specifying an immediate issuance deadline that the article does not contain. Identity papers establish identity for dealings with authorities and can help people access services and legal procedures. They are not automatically a passport, citizenship certificate, residence authorization, or permission to cross a border. Travel documents are addressed separately in Article 28. Refugees lawfully staying in the territory should receive documents for travel outside it unless compelling reasons of national security or public order require otherwise; the Convention's Schedule sets further terms. States may issue documents to other refugees and should give sympathetic consideration where refugees cannot obtain a document from the country of lawful residence. Article 28 does not impose a universal permanent-address or demonstrated-travel-need test as described in some summaries. Domestic application procedures and relevant reservations should be checked without confusing them with treaty wording. Lack of documentation can impede work, services, movement, and challenges to detention or removal. The distinction between identity and travel documents matters because access to one does not automatically establish entitlement to international entry or citizenship.
groups.mid: Article 27 of the 1951 Refugee Convention covers identity papers. A state must issue them to a refugee in its territory who lacks a valid travel document. Unlike some other articles, it does not say lawful stay is required. It sets no fixed deadline. Nor does it say the duty begins only at a formal event to confirm status. Identity papers show officials who you are. They may help with services, jobs, or legal cases. They are not automatically a passport, citizenship, residence permission, or a right to cross a border. Article 28 deals with travel documents. Refugees lawfully staying in a state should get them for travel abroad. Compelling national-security or public-order reasons can create an exception. The Convention's Schedule gives more terms. States may also issue them to other refugees. They should consider people who cannot get a document from the country where they lawfully live. The treaty does not set one permanent-address or necessary-journey test for everyone. Check local procedures and relevant treaty reservations. A lack of papers can block work, services, movement, or a challenge to detention or removal. Identity and travel documents have different purposes. Neither automatically gives citizenship or guarantees entry to another country.
groups.low: Article 27 of the 1951 Refugee Convention concerns identity papers. A state must give them to a refugee in its territory who has no valid travel document. The article does not say the person must first have lawful-stay status. It gives no fixed number of days for issuance. Nor does it say a formal recognition ceremony is the starting point. Identity papers help show officials who you are. They may help you deal with services, work, and legal cases. They are not automatically a passport or citizenship. They do not by themselves give permission to live in a place or cross a border. Article 28 deals with travel documents. A refugee lawfully staying in the country should get one for travel abroad, unless compelling national-security or public-order reasons prevent it. More terms are in the Convention's Schedule. States may give travel documents to other refugees too. They should consider people who cannot get a document from the country where they lawfully live. The treaty does not set one permanent-address or necessary-journey test for everyone. Local application rules and treaty reservations may matter. A lack of papers can make work, services, movement, and legal challenges harder. Keep the difference clear: identity papers show who you are; travel documents help with travel under separate rules. Neither makes you a citizen or guarantees that another country will admit you.
groups.source_review: Articles27/28 and travel-document exceptions checked against text.
groups.notes: Removed recognition-only and immediate-issuance conditions, passport-equivalence and invented permanent-address requirements.

groups.high: Article 34 of the 1951 Refugee Convention requires Contracting States, as far as possible, to facilitate refugees' assimilation and naturalization. Naturalization means acquiring the host state's nationality; social integration is related but not identical. The provision does not itself confer citizenship, establish a universal residence period, or require immediate approval regardless of national eligibility rules. It specifically calls for every effort to expedite naturalization proceedings and reduce charges and costs as far as possible. These procedural and financial elements matter alongside substantive access: unreasonable delay or unaffordable fees can make a formally available route ineffective. Domestic residence, language, documentation, and other requirements still need to be checked, together with measures adapting them to refugees' circumstances. Refugees may be unable to approach their country of origin safely or obtain documents that other applicants can readily supply. Facilitation can therefore involve accessible information, appropriate evidence alternatives, efficient processing, and justified fee reductions, without assuming that every example is expressly mandated in identical form by Article 34. Integration should not be described as an obligation to abandon religion, identity, or culture. The objective is a practicable route toward secure membership in society rather than indefinite administrative uncertainty. No fixed treaty deadline should be invented, and the clause's qualified duty to facilitate should not be misrepresented as an unconditional guarantee of a favorable citizenship decision.
groups.mid: Article 34 of the 1951 Refugee Convention says states must help refugees integrate and become citizens as far as possible. Becoming a citizen is called naturalization. Integration means taking part in society; the two are related but not the same. The article does not give citizenship at once, set one residence period, or promise every claim will succeed. It asks states to make every effort to speed up the process and reduce fees and costs as far as possible. Long waits and high fees can block a route that exists on paper. Check the country's residence, language, and document rules. Ask what help is offered to refugees. They may not be able to get papers from their old government safely. Clear advice, other forms of proof, lower fees, and prompt decisions can help. These are ways to offer support, not one identical list written into Article 34 for every state. Integration does not mean a person must give up religion, culture, or identity. The aim is a workable path to secure membership in society. The treaty gives no fixed deadline and does not guarantee a favorable citizenship decision.
groups.low: A refugee may want to become a citizen of the country where they live. That process is called naturalization. Article 34 of the 1951 Refugee Convention says states should help as far as possible. It covers integration and naturalization, which are related but different. The article does not give automatic citizenship. It does not set one waiting period for every country or promise approval. It says states should make every effort to speed up the process and reduce fees and costs as far as possible. Long delays and high costs can block a route that exists on paper. Check local rules for residence, language, documents, and other conditions. Ask what help is available for refugees. A refugee may not be able to ask their old government for papers without danger. Other proof, clear guidance, lower fees, and prompt decisions can help. These are possible ways to assist, not one identical list the treaty demands in every case. Integration is not a rule that you must give up your religion, culture, or identity. The aim is a workable route to secure membership in society. Do not rely on a made-up deadline. The treaty does not promise approval.
groups.source_review: Article34 checked, including often-omitted reduction of charges and costs.
groups.notes: Added fee/cost duty; avoided compulsory cultural assimilation and guaranteed citizenship implications.

groups.high: Article 22 of the 1951 Refugee Convention distinguishes elementary education from education beyond that level. For elementary education, Contracting States must accord refugees the same treatment as nationals. For other education, they must provide treatment as favorable as possible and at least no less favorable than that accorded to foreigners generally in the same circumstances. This includes access to study, recognition of foreign certificates, diplomas and degrees, fee and charge remission, and scholarships. Article 22 does not automatically extend its national-treatment clause to all secondary schooling, nor does it limit the second clause only to universities. The relevant educational level and local system must be identified. The foreigner comparison concerns foreigners generally in comparable circumstances, not an absolute right to the best benefit ever offered to any foreign national. Conversely, the Convention does not prohibit a state from treating refugees as favorably as citizens in higher education. It sets minimum protections rather than a ceiling on inclusion. Other human-rights instruments and domestic law may provide stronger educational rights, including for children. Practical access also depends on documentation, language support, and fair recognition processes, but specific accommodations should be distinguished from the express treaty wording. Education helps refugees rebuild their lives and participate in society. Assess the actual admissions, fee, scholarship, and qualification-recognition rules instead of assuming either universal citizen parity or unavoidable exclusion beyond primary school.
groups.mid: Article 22 of the 1951 Refugee Convention gives two standards for study. For elementary education, refugees must get the same treatment as citizens. For other education, states must give treatment as favorable as possible. At minimum, it must be no worse than the treatment of foreigners generally in the same circumstances. This covers entry to study, recognition of certificates and degrees, fee help, and scholarships. The first rule does not automatically cover every secondary school. The second is not only for universities. Check the level in the local system. The comparison with foreigners is not a right to every special benefit ever given to any foreign student. Similar conditions must be compared. A state can give refugees the same support as citizens in higher education. The treaty sets a minimum, not a ceiling. Other human-rights and national laws may give stronger rights, especially to children. Missing papers, a new language, and problems with past qualifications can block study. Help matters, but not every helpful step is expressly listed in Article 22. Check entry, fees, scholarships, and how past study is recognized. Do not assume everything is free or that support must end after primary school.
groups.low: Article 22 of the 1951 Refugee Convention covers school and study. For elementary education, refugees get the same treatment as citizens. After that, a state must give treatment as favorable as possible. It must be at least as good as that given to foreigners generally in the same circumstances. This includes entry to study and recognition of certificates and degrees from past study. It also covers help with fees and scholarships. A fee is what the school asks you to pay. A scholarship helps pay for study. The first rule does not cover all secondary schools by default. The second rule is not just for university study. Check the level in the local system. It is not a right to every special benefit any foreign student ever had. Compare similar cases. A state may give refugees the same help as citizens beyond primary school. The treaty sets a minimum. It does not ban more help. Other laws can give stronger rights, especially for children. Missing papers or a new language can make study hard. So can problems with past qualifications. Help with these is useful, but not every form of help is stated in Article 22. Check entry rules, fees, scholarships, and recognition of past study. Do not assume all study is free or that help must stop after primary school.
groups.source_review: Article22 distinction and its specific certificate/fee/scholarship coverage checked.
groups.notes: Corrected automatic secondary-school national parity and false claim citizen preferences cannot be extended to refugees.

groups.high: Article 26 of the 1951 Refugee Convention requires Contracting States to grant refugees lawfully in their territory the right to choose their place of residence and move freely within it, subject to regulations applicable to foreigners generally in the same circumstances. The lawful-presence qualification should not be omitted, but neither should the reference to foreigner regulations be treated as unlimited permission to impose arbitrary refugee-only restrictions. The comparator and the justification for any restriction matter. Domestic registration and residence procedures may be relevant, but the Convention does not establish a universal rule that employment is required for movement or that any registration lapse automatically suspends the right. Internal movement is distinct from admission across an international border, permanent immigration status, and permission to enter another country. Article 31 separately addresses refugees entering or present irregularly under its specified conditions. It limits movement restrictions to those necessary, for the period needed to regularize status or obtain admission elsewhere, and calls for a reasonable period and necessary facilities to obtain admission to another country. Other applicable human-rights rules can supply additional safeguards against arbitrary detention and movement restrictions. Practical questions about relocation, registration, or permits require the relevant domestic rules and individual circumstances, not an assumption of unrestricted sovereign discretion. The protection supports access to employment, services, family, and community life while preserving lawful, comparable restrictions within the treaty's limits.
groups.mid: Article 26 of the 1951 Refugee Convention protects movement. Refugees lawfully in the country can move and choose where to live. Rules for foreigners generally in the same circumstances may still apply. Officials do not have unlimited power. They must not impose arbitrary limits just on refugees. The right comparison and a sound reason for any limit matter. Local rules may require registration or a permit. But the treaty does not say each person needs a job before moving. Nor does it say a missed registration step always ends the right. Moving inside a country is different from crossing its border, gaining permanent residence, or entering another state. Article 31 has separate rules for people who enter or stay irregularly and meet its conditions. Movement limits must be necessary. They apply while lawful status or entry elsewhere is arranged. People should have reasonable time and needed facilities to seek entry elsewhere. Other human-rights rules may also guard against arbitrary detention and unfair movement limits. Check local law and your situation before moving. Do not assume all rules vanish. But state power is not unlimited either. This right helps people reach work and services. It helps them see family and join community life too.
groups.low: Article 26 of the 1951 Refugee Convention protects movement. It applies to refugees lawfully there. They can choose where to live and move around. Rules for foreigners generally in the same circumstances can still apply. Officials cannot use this to make any limit they want just for refugees. They need the right comparison and a sound reason. Local rules may call for registration or a permit. The treaty does not say you need a job before moving. One missed step does not always end the treaty right. Moving inside a country is not the same as crossing a border. It does not give permanent residence or entry to another state. Article 31 has separate rules for people who enter or stay irregularly and meet its conditions. Movement limits must be necessary while their status or entry elsewhere is arranged. They should have enough time and needed help to seek entry elsewhere. Other human-rights laws may guard against arbitrary detention. They may protect movement too. Check the local rules and your own case before moving. Do not assume there are no rules, or that officials have unlimited power. The right helps people reach jobs, services, family, and community life.
groups.source_review: Article26 lawful-in qualification and Article31 temporary restriction terms checked.
groups.notes: Removed invented employment prerequisite, automatic suspension and unfettered alien-regulation discretion.

groups.high: Article 20 of the 1951 Refugee Convention requires national treatment when a rationing system applies to the population at large and regulates the general distribution of products in short supply. A Contracting State must treat refugees like nationals within that system rather than assign inferior access solely because of refugee status. Rationing can allocate scarce necessities such as food or fuel during shortage, but Article 20 does not itself compel a state to introduce rationing or guarantee unlimited supplies. National treatment means applying the same relevant eligibility rules, need categories, and distribution standards. It does not necessarily require every person to receive an identical quantity regardless of age, household size, disability, or other legitimate criteria. Nor does the text insist on physically identical queues or prohibit delivery arrangements that improve access. The relevant question is whether refugees receive equivalent treatment under the scheme, not whether administration is identical in every detail. Documentation and enrollment procedures should not defeat that equality in practice. This is a refugee-law obligation of the Convention, rather than a rule limited to armed conflict under international humanitarian law. Broader rights to food and nondiscrimination may also matter, but should not be confused with Article 20's specific scope. Check the rationing scheme's rules and seek help from the responsible authority or a refugee-support service if exclusion or a lower allocation appears based solely on refugee status.
groups.mid: Article 20 of the 1951 Refugee Convention applies when a country has a rationing system for the population at large. Rationing shares products that are in short supply, such as food or fuel. Refugees must be treated like citizens under that system. They should not get less or be shut out just because they are refugees. The article does not force a country to start rationing, and it does not promise unlimited supplies. Equal treatment means the same relevant rules for eligibility, needs, and distribution. It does not mean that every person must receive exactly the same amount. A child, a large household, or a person with a particular need may fall into a different category, if the same rules apply to citizens and refugees. The treaty also does not require everyone to stand in the same physical queue. A different delivery route can be fair or improve access. What matters is equal treatment, not identical administration. Registration and document rules should not make equality impossible in practice. This is a refugee-law protection, not a rule that applies only in war. Other rights to food and fair treatment may add protection, but Article 20 has its own scope. Check the scheme's rules. If refugee status seems to be the only reason for exclusion or a smaller share, ask the responsible authority or a refugee-support service for help.
groups.low: Rationing is a way to share goods when there is not enough for everyone. It may cover food or fuel. Article 20 of the 1951 Refugee Convention says refugees must be treated like citizens when a rationing system serves the population at large. A refugee should not be left out or get less just because of that status. The article does not require a country to start rationing. It does not promise unlimited goods. The same relevant rules should apply to citizens and refugees. Those rules can take account of age, household size, or special needs. So equal treatment does not always mean the same amount for each person. Nor must everyone use the same queue or delivery point. A different route may make access easier. The test is fair, equal treatment under the scheme. Rules for registration and papers should not block that in practice. This is part of refugee law. It is not a right only during war. Other rights to food and fair treatment can matter too, but they are separate from Article 20's exact rule. Read the scheme's conditions or ask for an explanation. If you are denied a share only because you are a refugee, ask the authority or a refugee-support service for help.
groups.source_review: Article20 general-population rationing scope and national-treatment standard checked.
groups.notes: Corrected identical-per-capita allocation and same-queue mandates; clarified no duty to create rationing.

groups.high: Article 16 of the 1951 Refugee Convention establishes free access to courts in the territory of all Contracting States. Free access means the ability to use the courts without exclusion on refugee grounds; it is not a universal promise that every lawyer, filing, and proceeding costs nothing. In the state of habitual residence, a refugee must receive the same treatment as nationals regarding court access, including legal assistance and exemption from security for costs imposed on foreign litigants, known as cautio judicatum solvi. In other Contracting States, those matters are assessed by comparison with nationals of the refugee's country of habitual residence. These attachment-specific rules should not be collapsed into automatic citizen parity everywhere. Ordinary procedural requirements can apply, but must not nullify the relevant access guarantee. Court access can enable challenges to unlawful detention, contract claims, compensation claims, and protection of other rights, subject to jurisdiction and the available legal remedies. Article 16 itself does not establish a universal individual complaint court or guarantee success in every case. Legal-aid eligibility and practical assistance should be checked under domestic law and other applicable rights. Accessible information, interpretation where needed, and advice may be crucial to effective use of a legal remedy, although their precise legal basis can come from instruments beyond Article 16. Keep identity papers and case records where possible and seek qualified advice about the relevant court, deadlines, fees, and assistance.
groups.mid: Article 16 of the 1951 Refugee Convention protects court access in states that are parties. Free access does not mean every lawyer or court service costs nothing. In the country where a refugee usually lives, they get the same treatment as citizens for court access and legal aid. They also get the same exemption from a special costs deposit. This deposit is sometimes imposed on foreign claimants. The legal name is cautio judicatum solvi. In other treaty states, the comparison is different. It is with nationals of the refugee's country of usual residence. So citizen equality does not work in exactly the same way everywhere. Normal court rules may apply. They must not defeat access. A court may hear claims about unlawful detention, contracts, or compensation, if it has the right powers. Article 16 does not create a world court for all refugee complaints. Nor does it promise success in every case. Check local legal-aid rules, fees, deadlines, and the right court. Clear advice and an interpreter may be needed; other laws may give those rights. Keep identity papers and case records where you can. Seek qualified help before a deadline passes.
groups.low: Article 16 of the 1951 Refugee Convention gives a right to use courts in states that are parties. Free access does not mean all lawyers and court services are free. Where you usually live, you must get the same treatment as citizens for court access and legal help. This includes the same exemption from a special costs deposit for foreign claimants. The legal name is cautio judicatum solvi. In another treaty state, the comparison is with nationals of the country where you usually live. So the citizen rule does not work in the same way everywhere. You still need to follow proper court rules. They must not wipe out the access right. A court may hear a case about detention, a contract, or compensation if it has the right powers. The article does not create one world court for all complaints. It does not promise you will win. Ask which court to use. Check deadlines, fees, and legal-aid rules. Advice and an interpreter may help. Other laws may give those rights. Keep papers about your identity and case when you can. Seek help before a deadline passes.
groups.source_review: All three Article16 paragraphs checked; free access distinguished from free-of-cost universal representation.
groups.notes: Corrected universal fee-free implication and citizen-parity scope; no invented treaty complaint mechanism.
